questions.q: What does it mean for two orientation-preserving self-homeomorphisms $\varphi, \psi$ of an oriented surface $S$ to represent the same element of $\mathrm{Mod}(S)$?
choices: They are equal as set-theoretic maps $S\to S$.
They induce the same automorphism of $\pi_1(S)$.
There is an isotopy — a continuous path of homeomorphisms — connecting $\varphi$ to $\psi$.
They have the same Lefschetz number.
questions.explain: $\mathrm{Mod}(S) = \pi_0\,\mathrm{Homeo}^+(S)$ is the group of isotopy classes. Pointwise equality is too strict; same induced action on $\pi_1$ is closer (and on surfaces equivalent, by Baer / Dehn–Nielsen–Baer) but the original definition is via isotopy.

An orientation-preserving self-homeomorphism of $T^2$ acts on $H_1(T^2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$ by an element of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ of determinant $+1$, i.e. by an element of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. This linearisation is faithful, giving an isomorphism $\mathrm{Mod}(T^2)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

questions.q: Select all properties of $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$ that hold for every $g\ge 2$.
choices: Acts properly discontinuously on Teichmüller space $\mathcal{T}(\Sigma_g)$
Equals the orientation-preserving isometry group of any hyperbolic structure on $\Sigma_g$
Surjects onto $\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z})$ via its action on $H_1(\Sigma_g)$
questions.explain: $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$ is finitely presented (Wajnryb / Hatcher–Thurston), acts properly discontinuously on $\mathcal{T}$ with quotient $\mathcal{M}_g$, and its action on $H_1\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ preserves the algebraic intersection form, giving the surjection $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z})$ (kernel = the Torelli group). It is infinite for $g\ge 1$, and the isometry group of a hyperbolic structure is finite — only finite-order classes preserve any single metric.

questions.q: Let $\gamma\subset\Sigma_g$ be an essential simple closed curve. What is the order of the Dehn twist $T_\gamma$ in $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$?
questions.explain: Essential simple closed curves yield Dehn twists of infinite order. The fastest way to see this: $T_\gamma$ acts on $H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb{Z})$ as a transvection $x\mapsto x + \langle x,[\gamma]\rangle [\gamma]$, which has infinite order on the symplectic lattice whenever $[\gamma]\ne 0$. Bounding curves act trivially on $H_1$ but are still infinite-order in $\mathrm{Mod}$.

questions.q: How many Dehn twists are required in the Humphries minimal generating set for $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_4)$? (Genus $g = 4$.)
questions.explain: Humphries' theorem: $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$ is generated by twists about $2g+1$ curves, and no smaller set of Dehn twists generates. For $g=4$: $2\cdot 4 + 1 = 9$.

questions.q: Order these relations in $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$ from local (smallest support) to global.
items: Disjoint commuting: $T_\alpha T_\beta = T_\beta T_\alpha$ when $\alpha\cap\beta=\emptyset$
Braid: $T_\alpha T_\beta T_\alpha = T_\beta T_\alpha T_\beta$ when $|\alpha\cap\beta|=1$
Lantern: 4 boundary twists = 3 internal twists on a 4-holed sphere
Hyperelliptic involution centralizes the generating chain on $\Sigma_2$
questions.explain: Disjoint commuting needs only an annular neighbourhood of each curve. Braid needs the union of two annular neighbourhoods (intersecting once). Lantern needs a 4-holed sphere — substantially larger. The hyperelliptic relation is global, characterising the entire surface for $g=2$.

questions.q: By the Nielsen–Thurston classification, every $\varphi\in\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$ is exactly one of three types. Which is NOT one of them?
questions.explain: The trichotomy is finite-order / reducible / pseudo-Anosov. The Lefschetz number is a continuous invariant of $\varphi$ but does not figure in the classification.

questions.q: If $\varphi$ is pseudo-Anosov with dilatation $\lambda = 2$, what is the topological entropy $h(\varphi) = \log\lambda$? (To 3 decimal places.)
questions.explain: $h(\varphi) = \log\lambda = \log 2 \approx 0.6931$. The topological entropy of a pseudo-Anosov mapping class equals the log of its dilatation — this is the surface analogue of the entropy formula $h(A) = \log|\lambda_+|$ for hyperbolic toral automorphisms.

questions.q: Spot the flawed step in this argument that no $\varphi\in\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_2)$ is pseudo-Anosov.
steps: Then $\lambda$ is the largest eigenvalue of the action on $H_1(\Sigma_2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^4$.
But every element of $\mathrm{Sp}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ has all eigenvalues on the unit circle or pairs $\{\mu, \mu^{-1}\}$.
So $\lambda \le 1$, contradicting $\lambda > 1$ — pseudo-Anosov maps cannot exist on $\Sigma_2$.
questions.explain: Step 2 is wrong: the dilatation $\lambda$ is the spectral radius of the action on a measured-foliation train-track, NOT on $H_1(\Sigma_g)$. The action on $H_1$ lives in $\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z})$ which can certainly have eigenvalues of modulus $>1$, but more importantly, $\lambda$ is computed from train-track expansion, not homology. Pseudo-Anosov maps DO exist on $\Sigma_2$ — the minimum dilatation there is the largest root of $x^4-x^3-x^2-x+1\approx 1.7221$.

questions.q: What is the real dimension of Teichmüller space $\mathcal{T}(\Sigma_g)$ for genus $g = 5$?
In Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates with respect to a pants decomposition, what does a Dehn twist $T_{\gamma_i}$ about the $i$-th pants curve do?
choices: $\tau_i \mapsto \tau_i + \ell_i$, leaving lengths and other twists fixed
Acts as the identity on Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates
questions.explain: A Dehn twist about a pants curve $\gamma_i$ shifts the twist parameter $\tau_i$ by exactly the length $\ell_i$ — the geodesic distance one needs to traverse one full re-gluing — while leaving every other Fenchel–Nielsen coordinate fixed. This is what makes the action of the cyclic subgroup $\langle T_{\gamma_i}\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathcal{T}$ a translation along the $\tau_i$-axis.

questions.q: Match each piece of moduli data with its dimension or invariant.
left: Number of pants curves in a pants decomposition of $\Sigma_g$
Number of Humphries Dehn-twist generators of $\mathrm{Mod}(\Sigma_g)$
questions.explain: Teichmüller space is real-$(6g-6)$ dimensional; the moduli space is complex-$(3g-3)$ dimensional. Both numbers $3g-3$ count pants curves: each pants decomposition of $\Sigma_g$ uses exactly $3g-3$ disjoint simple closed curves (cutting $\Sigma_g$ into $2g-2$ thrice-punctured spheres). The Humphries generating count $2g+1$ is unrelated.

questions.q: By Freedman's theorem, a closed simply-connected topological 4-manifold $X$ is determined by which combination of invariants?
choices: Its intersection form $Q_X$ together with the Kirby–Siebenmann invariant $\mathrm{ks}(X)\in\mathbb{Z}/2$
questions.explain: Freedman (1982): the homeomorphism type of a closed simply-connected topological 4-manifold is determined by the unimodular intersection form $Q_X$ on $H_2(X;\mathbb{Z})$ together with the Kirby–Siebenmann obstruction in $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Every odd unimodular form occurs (with both KS values), and every even one occurs subject to $\mathrm{ks}=0$ when $Q$ is even ($\mathrm{ks}=1$ corresponds to non-smoothable cases like Freedman's $E_8$-manifold).

questions.q: Donaldson's diagonalisability theorem says: if $X$ is a closed smooth simply-connected 4-manifold whose intersection form $Q_X$ is definite (signature $= \pm b_2$), then $Q_X$ is diagonal $\langle\pm 1, \dots, \pm 1\rangle$ over $\mathbb{Z}$. Which Freedman manifold does this rule out as smoothable?
choices: The Freedman manifold $M_{E_8}$ with intersection form the $E_8$ lattice
questions.explain: $E_8$ is even, definite, and unimodular — Freedman produces a topological 4-manifold realising it, but Donaldson's theorem forbids any smooth structure (since $E_8$ is not diagonal over $\mathbb{Z}$). The other choices are all smoothable: $\mathbb{CP}^2$ has $Q=\langle 1\rangle$ (diagonal), $S^2\times S^2$ has $Q=H$ (indefinite, so Donaldson does not apply), K3 has signature $-16$ but indefinite form $2(-E_8)\oplus 3H$.

questions.q: Which of the following are TRUE about smooth 4-manifolds (and false in every other dimension)?
choices: There exist uncountably many smooth structures on $\mathbb{R}^4$.
The smooth $h$-cobordism theorem fails: $h$-cobordant smooth simply-connected 4-manifolds need not be diffeomorphic.
Some closed simply-connected topological 4-manifolds carry no smooth structure.
questions.explain: All three exotic-4 phenomena hold uniquely in dimension four: Taubes (uncountable smooth $\mathbb{R}^4$s), Donaldson (smooth $h$-cobordism fails — $E(2,3)$ vs $E(1,1)$ etc.), and Freedman+Donaldson together (Freedman's $E_8$ manifold has no smooth structure). Parallelisability fails for $\mathbb{CP}^2$ already (non-zero Stiefel–Whitney classes).

mcg-casson.title: Casson invariant and the Donaldson preview

questions.q: The Casson invariant $\lambda(\Sigma)$ of a homology 3-sphere $\Sigma$ is defined as half the algebraic count of which intersection?
choices: Lagrangian intersection of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ representation varieties of two handlebodies in a Heegaard splitting
Algebraic count of fixed points of a generic diffeomorphism
Intersection product of two Seifert surfaces
questions.explain: Heegaard split $\Sigma = H_+ \cup_{F_g} H_-$. The irreducible $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ representation varieties $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{irr}}(H_\pm)$ embed as Lagrangian half-dimensional submanifolds of the symplectic moduli $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{irr}}(F_g)$ (Atiyah–Bott). For generic splittings their intersection is finite; $\lambda$ counts these signed intersections, divided by 2 to convert from $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ to $\mathrm{SO}(3)$.

questions.q: Casson's surgery formula: $\lambda(\Sigma_{+1}(K)) - \lambda(\Sigma) = \frac{1}{2}\Delta_K''(1)$. For the trefoil knot $K = 3_1$ in $S^3$, the Alexander polynomial is $\Delta(t) = t - 1 + t^{-1}$, so $\Delta''(1) = 2$. Compute $\lambda(S^3_{+1}(3_1))$.
questions.explain: $\lambda(S^3) = 0$. Surgery formula: $\lambda(S^3_{+1}(3_1)) = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2 = 1$. (Sign conventions vary by author; many normalisations give $\lambda(\Sigma(2,3,7)) = -1$ — the Brieskorn sphere $\Sigma(2,3,7)$ is realised as $-1$-surgery on the right-handed trefoil. The surgery formula recovers this with the appropriate sign.)

questions.q: Complete the chain that shows the Casson invariant refines the Rohlin invariant.
steps: The Rohlin invariant $\mu(\Sigma)\in\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the signature mod 16 (divided by 8) of any spin 4-manifold bounding $\Sigma$.
The Casson invariant $\lambda(\Sigma)\in\mathbb{Z}$ counts irreducible $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ flat connections (with signs) in a Heegaard splitting.
questions.explain: Casson's congruence: $\lambda(\Sigma) \bmod 2 = \mu(\Sigma)\in\mathbb{Z}/2$. This was the first proof of triangulation-independence of the Rohlin invariant via gauge-theoretic / representation-variety methods, and it shows $\lambda$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-valued lift of the older $\mathbb{Z}/2$-invariant. Floer later refined this further into instanton homology, an entire graded abelian group whose Euler characteristic is $2\lambda(\Sigma)$.
